name: Antigua and Barbuda

facts.religion: Christian, mostly Anglican and other Protestant

snapshot: A twin-island Caribbean state built on tourism, where Gaston Browne won a landslide fourth term in April 2026.
culture: Antigua claims a beach for every day of the year. Carnival, held in late July and early August to mark emancipation from slavery in 1834, is the biggest event of the year, with calypso and steel pan competitions. Cricket is a passion; Sir Viv Richards, one of the game's greatest batsmen, is Antiguan, and the national stadium bears his name.
society: Tourism, especially cruise ships and luxury resorts, accounts for most of the economy. Barbuda, the sister island, was devastated by Hurricane Irma in 2017, and a dispute over land rights there has pitted Barbudans against the government. A citizenship-by-investment programme is a big source of revenue.
situation: Gaston Browne's Antigua and Barbuda Labour Party won the 30 April 2026 general election by a landslide, giving him a fourth term after a narrower win in 2023. Browne has been a prominent voice for climate finance and slavery reparations and has said a referendum on becoming a republic could follow.
power: A parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm. The prime minister leads the majority in the 17-seat House of Representatives; a governor-general represents the king.

leaders.state: King Charles III, represented by a governor-general
leaders.gov: Prime Minister Gaston Browne, since 2014, re-elected April 2026

Ducana, sweet potato dumplings, with saltfish

Whether to replace the king with a president

story: Britain colonised Antigua in 1632 and turned it into a sugar island worked by enslaved Africans; Nelson's Dockyard was the Royal Navy's Caribbean base. Slavery ended in 1834. Independent in 1981, it was dominated for decades by the Bird family.
timeline: The Bird family's party loses power after nearly 30 years
